evidence.text: The entry traces object ‘bottom/back’ uses from heel, citing 清稗類鈔·鑒賞類 (“每冊之跟”), and gives shoe heel as a continuing use. It reports follow as a later common sense and quotes 正字通·足部, “俗謂隨行曰跟”; later cited examples include 三国演义 chapter 28 and 红楼梦 chapter 43. It then explains attendant/servant and marriage senses from follow, and later prepositional/object and conjunction uses with examples from 红楼梦, 老残游记, 龙须沟, and 小二黑结婚. evidence.text: This entry identifies 跟 as an 艮-series phonetic graph and lists 跟 Old Chinese *kɯːn and 艮 *kɯːns in Zhengzhang (2003). It gives 跟 Middle Chinese fanqie 古痕切 and category 見開一痕平, with Mandarin gēn and Cantonese gan1; it gives 艮 Mandarin readings gèn, gěn (among others) and Cantonese gan3. In the stated reconstruction, the related initial and rhyme support a phonetic role despite the departing tone suffix on 艮. The source also reports 跟 as cognate with 根 (Old Chinese *kɯːn), attributed to Wang (1982), but no primary text supporting that cognacy was inspected here.

gaps: No dated oracle-bone, bronze, or excavated manuscript attestation of 跟 was located. The consulted CUHK entry lists no oracle-bone or bronze example and only one small-seal example; this database absence is not proof that no earlier occurrence exists.

The alternative form 𣥦 is attributed by Shuowen to a shape with 止 instead of 足, but the evidence reviewed does not establish whether it is contemporary, earlier, or later than 跟. Classification as an earlier ancestor would be unsupported.

The proposed sound element is 艮, not a whole-graph loan. The phonological evidence supports a sound role; no separate depicted object, source word, or borrowed-word account is implicated by this analysis.

Heel-to-object-back and heel-to-follow extensions are plausible and described by the character database, but a complete dated sequence establishing the semantic links and first uses was not recovered. The object-back citation from 清稗類鈔 and later literary examples need edition-level dating.
The “跟 and 根 cognate” claim is attributed to Wang (1982) by Wiktionary; that cited argument was not inspected, and the relation should remain an attributed proposal rather than established fact.

Kotobank’s account that 艮 graphically signifies retreat through an evil-eye taboo conflicts in emphasis with the simple phonetic-component analysis and lacks corroboration among inspected paleographic sources. No glyph image was visually inspected.

No dated oracle-bone, bronze, or excavated manuscript attestation was located in the inspected sources. The CUHK page records no oracle or bronze examples and one small-seal example; that database coverage does not prove earlier forms never existed.

Shuowen records 𣥦 as an alternative form using 止, but the evidence inspected does not establish whether it precedes, follows, or is contemporary with 跟. Treating it as an ancestor would overstate the evidence.
The phonetic analysis concerns 艮 as a component of 跟. No whole-graph phonetic loan or borrowed source word is implicated, so evidence about an original depicted object's name is not applicable.

The sources report heel, object-back, follow, attendant, and prepositional or conjunction senses, but a dated semantic chain and first attestations for each extension were not independently established. The received 焦氏易林 wording is not itself a secure date for the composition or for that wording's entry into the text.
Wiktionary attributes 跟/根 cognacy to Wang (1982); that argument was not inspected. Kotobank's alternative word-family discussion is not independently corroborated here.

No historical glyph image is proposed: actual searches and page inspections did not establish an image candidate for 跟 with a verified identity and reuse provenance. The PDF table is only a lead, not a selected query-interface image.
